NOTE: There’s been some confusion about whether this video is correct, so I want to clear that up. I completely understand the points raised, but rest assured, the methods shown here are the best way to get the most out of your display.

I highly recommend this in-depth video by HDTVTest, which explains the technical details behind this approach: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FwcSCgW47rY. If you have a spare 20 minutes, give it a watch after this one. Vincent is a professional TV calibrator with years of experience so you can trust his insights.

Sony’s instructions use the ‘barely visible’ method because it’s simpler for the average user to understand and still yields a good result, but it does tell the PS5 your display has a lower peak brightness and higher minimum luminance than it actually does. The method(s) in the video on the other hand, ensures you get the full dynamic range of your TV/monitor.

I hope this clears up any confusion & you find this video useful; I've certainly noticed a big difference since setting this up properly myself. 😊 Also, Merry Christmas! 🎅

O recomendado para a grande maioria dos jogadores é usar a opção *Ativado quando compatível* (On When Supported).
Aqui está o porquê de essa ser a melhor escolha e como cada uma das opções afeta a sua imagem:
### 1. Ativado quando compatível (Recomendado)
Essa opção faz com que o PS5 mude de comportamento dinamicamente com base no conteúdo que você está assistindo ou jogando.
 * *Como funciona:* Se o jogo ou aplicativo (como Netflix ou YouTube) foi feito em HDR, o PS5 ativa o HDR. Se o jogo é antigo ou não tem suporte (SDR), o PS5 desativa o HDR e entrega a imagem original.
 * *Vantagem:* Você sempre verá a imagem **exatamente como os desenvolvedores a criaram**. Jogos em SDR manterão as cores corretas, sem distorções, e jogos em HDR aproveitarão todo o potencial de brilho e contraste da sua TV.
### 2. Sempre ativado
Essa opção força o PS5 a converter absolutamente tudo o que sai dele para um sinal HDR, mesmo que o conteúdo original seja SDR.
 * *Como funciona:* O console tenta "adivinhar" e mapear as cores de um jogo comum para o espectro HDR.
 * *Desvantagem:* Isso costuma causar uma distorção chamada black crush (onde os tons escuros perdem detalhes e viram um borrão preto) ou deixar as cores excessivamente estouradas, artificiais e saturadas (como tons de pele muito vermelhos ou laranjas). Além disso, a imagem pode parecer estranhamente lavada ou escura em telas que não possuem um gerenciamento perfeito dessa conversão forçada.
### Resumo da ópera
| Opção | O que acontece na prática | Veredito |
|---|---|---|
| *Ativado quando compatível* | Imagem precisa e natural. HDR só liga quando o jogo realmente tem suporte. | *Escolha ideal* para a melhor fidelidade visual. |
| *Sempre ativado* | Força HDR em tudo. Pode estragar o visual de jogos SDR antigos ou retrocompatíveis. | **Evite**, a menos que você goste de cores artificialmente vibrantes. |
> *Dica extra:* Sempre que selecionar "Ativado quando compatível", certifique-se de ir logo abaixo no menu em *Ajustar HDR* para calibrar os níveis de brilho máximo e preto do console de acordo com o painel da sua TV. Isso garante que os destaques brilhantes não fiquem "estourados" e os detalhes nas sombras apareçam perfeitamente.

comments.text:
Turn HGIG on (mandatory) and use below calibration guidelines for OLED, Mini-LED,QLED or similar tvs.

For Sony’s first party games (like Spiderman 2 , GOW Ragnarok etc.) that uses PS5 HDR calibration menu:
Screen 1 & 2 => Make sun barely visible (Doing this will still allow first party games to display tv’s max peak brightness without clipping in highlights).
3rd Screen => One click up from the lowest value to make the sun barely barely visible - Doing this won't raise black level in first party games. Instead It will give nice shadow details in dark/scenes areas while still displaying inky/deep blacks.

Third Party Games(Like Hogwarts legacy, Jedi Survivor, etc) that uses PS5 HDR calibration Menu:
Sreen 1 & 2 => Make sun completely invisible (One step higher from barely visible or else third party games won’t output your tv’s max peak brightness).
3rd Screen => All the way down to zero clicks (anything other than zero clicks will turn deep blacks to greyish blacks on third party games).

Note: To make most out of PS5 HDR gaming, Ensure that your tv supports HDMI 2.1  and is an OLED screen OR LCD/LED that has local dimming algorithm. Anything other than this will result in washed out HDR experience

Most of these videos on the best settings for your TV are misleading as most games do not use the system level HDR settings to calculate the HDR10 metadata you see in games. 

At best these settings govern the HDR of the display page of the game and videos that play in the PS store which support HDR. In truth....there are only a handful of games that use the system level HDR10 setting, namely the Insomniac Spiderman games (which is why its the only game shown in this video) and a few others. Every other game uses the in game HDR10 settings for the metadata and are the only settings that need to be properly calibrated for HDR. 

If anything your display settings control things like color saturation, overall screen brightness and the contrast (the difference between the darkest parts of the display and the brightest parts.) Everything else is controled by the in game HDR menus and should be adjusted on a game by game basis. 

In general there are things at a display level you will want to be mindful of....brightness does not make HDR brighter. Most of these videos are some person playing in torch mode (max brightness) which is only good for fighting background light sources. Its also why the max brightness of your TV doesn't matter for games and why colors appear washed out. If you are playing in max brightness in a dark room 9 times out of ten you are why the game looks washed out when using HDR, because the brightness is past the point of fighting reflections of outside light sources and is starting to make colors appear less saturatured than they actually are. You should set the display brightness and color saturation to a point where colors look rich, not dull or overly garish. This is going to be different for every display and for every room as the lighting conditions of your space will have a big impact here. Also with contrast, you should set the contrast to a point where black apears black given your room lighting. You want to find a point where objects in the dark are not completely crushed but not so bright where your blacks are grey. Again this is going to vary based on display and outside lighting conditions. 

Once you have your display values you never need to change them for games as everything else with how the game looks in HDR will vome down to how you vonfigur the in game HDR setting. In game you want to be using the directions that are given to achieve the best image the developer intends. If it says barely visible it means barely visible....clipping past that point will cause black crush. For brightness, you want to make sure that you maintain detail in the brightess parts of the scene...never clip past that point as that is where colors will start to get washed out or you can create white crush which is where you can't see other objects in a bright scene. 

If done right the game should look natural....not like a cartoon and not like a dull black and white photo. For gaming displays matter very little and things like Dynamic tone mapping will make it more difficult to get the few settings the TV does control right. While DTM does make the screen brighter again it is important to note that brightness is not always better since it does more to wash out color than it does to make your screen appear to have more contrast ratio. Its also why you feel you have to turn the color up to cartoon levels to get deep color saturation. 

As for the few games that do use the system level HDR you want to be one click past barely visible on an OLED on the white screens and barely visible on a LED TV. The reason is because OLED lighting comes from the pixel itself vs an LED TV which uses a backlight. LED tv's are generally better for a bright room or for people who game with the lights very bright and OLED is better for darker room.

This should cover those as it's a general guide for all displays! :) I see you mentioned the QN90C in a different comment, but QN90D here, so I'll just give you the best for both. If you want to know the how for doing this for non HGIG displays, I go through it at about 1:20 onwards, and you want to use that graph based on your peak 10% brightness window of the TV in HDR gaming (found on RTINGS.com).

QN90C: Has a 10% peak of 1996 nits, so from the graphic, that will round up to the 2000 nits option which wants 20 clicks. So for steps 1 and 2, go to the very lowest option, then from there, click up on the d-pad 20 times for each. For step 3, set it to the minimum value.

QN90D: Has a 10% peak of 2109 nits, so from the graphic, this would round up to the 2300 nits option which wants 21 clicks. So for steps 1 and 2, go to the very lowest option, then from there, click up on the d-pad 21 times for each. For step 3, set it to the minimum value. Note that because this isn't muuuch higher than the 20 steps option, you might want to try 20 steps too and just check which is best.

Hope that helps!
